The Cuzco warbler, Myiothlypis chrysogaster, is a small Neotropical passerine in the family Parulidae, and recent field studies have begun to characterize its basic physiological parameters. Basal metabolic rate measured under standard resting conditions in post-absorptive individuals reached 50.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 50.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the ambient temperature was carefully maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively high metabolic output, recorded in active adults, is consistent with the energetic demands of a foraging strategy that relies on gleaning insects from dense understory vegetation. At the onset of independent life, newly hatched nestlings emerge with an initial wet weight averaging 4.2 grams [Ww0 = 4.2 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial developmental mode characteristic of this lineage. Data collected from a marked population in the humid montane forests of southern Peru suggest that these early-life values serve as a foundation for the species' rapid growth trajectory.

Reproductive parameters of Myiothlypis chrysogaster indicate a slow pace of life for a bird of its size, likely shaped by the stable but resource-limited environment of its Andean cloud forest habitat. Females typically produce 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], a modest fecundity that is paired with a single annual nesting attempt [F_R_i = single annual nesting attempt], resulting in a total of 2 offspring per year per breeding female. Eggs are incubated for a period of approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days] at a nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other thlypine warblers. The careful thermal regulation of the clutch during incubation is critical for successful embryonic development in the cool, damp microclimate of the montane forest understory.

Under typical active-phase body temperatures of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 12 days [tx = 12 days], a brief nestling period that allows young to escape the high predation risk inherent to ground- or low-shrub nesting. Juveniles then enter a period of rapid somatic growth, reaching the ultimate female wet weight of 11.2 grams [Wwi = 11.2 grams] within their first several months. This adult body mass, which is comparable to that of other medium-bodied parulids, stabilizes after the completion of skeletal development and the accumulation of sufficient fat reserves. The relatively early departure from the nest, measured at just 12 days [tx = 12 days], is an adaptation that trades off prolonged parental care for increased survival of the brood through reduced nest exposure.

Despite becoming physiologically mature relatively early, first reproductive attempts are usually deferred. Longevity data for the species reveal a moderate maximum life span, with the oldest documented individuals in the field surviving 10 years [am = 10 years] at a typical active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This life span, combined with the species' low annual reproductive output of a single clutch of two eggs yearly, yields a slow life-history pace that is typical of many tropical montane passerines. The maximum of 10 years contrasts with the shorter lifespans seen in some temperate warblers, highlighting the potential role of reduced extrinsic mortality in the stable Andean environment. Taken together, these demographic and physiological data paint a picture of Myiothlypis chrysogaster as a species that invests heavily in each reproductive attempt, enabled by a reasonably long adult life span but constrained by a modest clutch size. Future work should focus on quantifying adult survival rates and dispersal distances to fully understand the population dynamics that govern this species' persistence in its fragmented cloud-forest habitat.
